question: On 21 February 2024, a Spanish journalist disclosed the details of a talk1 given by Manuel García Castellón, a judge at the Spanish National Court. During the talk, Judge García Castellón revealed to the audience that, while serving as a liaison judge in France, he misled the French authorities during a meeting in Bordeaux by falsely claiming that a dangerous criminal sought by France was hiding in Spain.

Judge García Castellón explained that his motive for deceiving the French authorities was to compel them to agree to a Security Agreement between Spain and France, known as the Malaga Agreement, dated 26 November 20022. In the light of this admission: 1.
Does the Commission intend to initiate any form of investigation into the deception by the Spanish authorities concerning judicial cooperation between Member States in criminal matters?

How does the Commission view the impact of this type of deception on the principle of loyal cooperation in criminal matters, as enshrined in Article 82 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union?
Does the Commission consider that actions of this type on the part of a judge are compatible with the principles of the rule of law enshrined in Article 2 of the Treaty on European Union?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (31.5.2024) The Commission has no competence to intervene in matters of judicial cooperation between the Member States that do not fall within the scope of the EU acquis on judicial cooperation, which, in criminal matters, is based on Article 82 of the Treaty on the Functioning of the European Union (TFEU).

The so called ‘Malaga Agreement’ of 26 November 2002 concerning readmission of persons residing without authorisation is a bilateral cooperation agreement concluded between two Member States without any basis in EU law, and thus cannot be considered to fall within the competence of the Commission nor does it implicate the principle of sincere cooperation established in Article 4(3) of the TFEU.
